strengths: The paper identifies a relevant problem: frozen visual encoders are task-agnostic, while ordinary text prompts may be poorly grounded in simulated control imagery. The proposed combination of task-level learned prompts and frame-specific visual prompts is intuitive and technically plausible.

The evaluation covers 12 tasks across three established suites (DMC, MetaWorld, and Adroit). ORCA improves the reported mean over the null-conditioned SCR baseline from 68.3 to 74.3 on DMC, 90.4 to 95.2 on MetaWorld, and 58.0 to 65.3 on Adroit.

The component ablation is informative: on DMC, task and visual prompts individually reach means of 69.8 and 70.5, while their combination reaches 74.3. Layer and timestep ablations, attention visualizations, and latency/parameter reporting further help characterize the method.
The manuscript is generally well organized, and its figures clearly communicate the motivation, architecture, and qualitative behavior.
weaknesses: The central attribution is confounded by the addition of a strong DINOv2 visual encoder and 10.6M learnable parameters. There is no DINOv2-only baseline, direct DINO-to-policy baseline, or late-fusion DINOv2+SCR baseline. Consequently, the experiments do not establish that cross-attention conditioning, rather than simply supplying DINOv2 features and extra capacity, causes the gains. This is the main material weakness.

Reported results are internally inconsistent. The default t=0 results in Appendix Table 6 have a DMC mean of 70.8, including Reacher-easy 71.9, whereas Tables 1 and 5 report 74.3 and 87.6 for the same default method. Figure 1 reports ORCA means of 96.3 on MetaWorld and 64.7 on Adroit, while Tables 2 and 3 report 95.2 and 65.3. Repeated entries in Tables 1 and 4 also have different standard deviations. These discrepancies materially weaken confidence in the empirical evidence.

Claims of significantly surpassing all baselines and obtaining state of the art on every task are overstated. Several results are ties, such as 44.0 on Adroit Relocate and 100.0 on Drawer-open, while other advantages are tiny relative to three-seed variability, such as 89.1 versus 89.0 on Walker-stand. No statistical tests or confidence intervals support the significance claim.

The explanation that text prompts fail because of a web-to-control domain gap remains speculative. Evidence consists mainly of two qualitative attention examples, and the tested captions are static task descriptions rather than frame-level captions. There is no quantitative grounding evaluation or controlled experiment separating domain gap from caption specificity and temporal variation.

Reproducibility is insufficient. The policy architecture, optimizer, learning rates, batch size, image preprocessing, DINOv2 variant, exact construction and positional treatment of visual tokens, evaluation episode count, and checkpoint-selection protocol are not specified. Reporting the best success rate among periodic online evaluations may also introduce selection bias without a separate validation protocol.

The compression-layer pseudocode applies BatchNorm2d(hidden_dim) after a convolution whose output has compress_dim channels, which is dimensionally inconsistent unless those values happen to match. Together with notation errors in the conditioning equation, this leaves important implementation details ambiguous.

The method roughly doubles SCR latency from 26 ms to 48 ms and adds a second large encoder, yet it is evaluated only in fixed simulated tasks. There is no evidence on real-robot transfer, visual perturbations, unseen viewpoints, or task generalization to justify broader robustness or usefulness claims.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: adapting frozen pretrained visual representations to individual control tasks without fine-tuning the large diffusion backbone. The combination of learned task tokens and frame-conditioned visual tokens is simple and potentially useful.

The evaluation covers 12 simulated tasks from three distinct suites—DeepMind Control, MetaWorld, and Adroit—and reports three-seed means and standard deviations. ORCA obtains the best aggregate score in every suite: 74.3 versus 70.7 on DMC, 95.2 versus 93.1 on MetaWorld, and 65.3 versus 58.0 on Adroit.

The component ablation in Table 4 supports complementarity between task and visual prompts: using both produces a 74.3 DMC mean, compared with 69.8 for task prompts alone, 70.5 for visual prompts alone, and 68.3 without either.

The paper includes relevant diagnostics, including prompt cross-attention visualizations, layer and timestep ablations, latency and parameter measurements, and comparisons with several textual-conditioning alternatives. The manuscript is generally readable and visually clear.
weaknesses: The central comparison is materially confounded by ORCA's use of a frozen DINOv2 encoder to generate visual prompts. There is no DINOv2-only policy baseline, no direct use of DINOv2 features, and no parameter-matched adapter baseline. Consequently, the experiments do not establish whether the gains come from the proposed diffusion-conditioning mechanism or simply from adding a strong second visual representation and additional learned projection capacity.

The statistical support is weaker than the claims suggest. Results use only three seeds, provide no significance tests or uncertainty for aggregate means, and many task-level improvements are small relative to reported variation—for example, 89.1 versus 89.0 on Walker-stand and 87.6 versus 87.1 on Reacher-easy. MetaWorld is near saturation, and the Adroit aggregate gain is largely driven by one of only two tasks. The assertion that ORCA significantly surpasses prior methods across all tasks is therefore overstated; several results are ties or effectively indistinguishable.

The evaluation selects the best success rate among periodic online evaluations on MetaWorld and Adroit. Selecting checkpoints using the reported evaluation environment creates optimistic test-selection bias unless a separate validation protocol is used, which is not described. Layer and timestep choices also appear to be selected using performance on the same DMC tasks ultimately reported.

The claimed explanation for textual prompts—domain-gap-induced erroneous grounding—is not adequately demonstrated. It rests mainly on selected attention-map examples, without a quantitative grounding metric, controlled domain-gap experiment, or evidence that attention quality causes policy performance. Only fixed task captions are tested, so the experiments also do not broadly establish that textual or frame-specific language conditioning is ineffective.

The framing around dynamic information is imprecise. Each visual prompt is computed from a single current frame, with no explicit temporal or motion modeling. Changes in attention across independently processed frames do not demonstrate that the representation captures dynamics rather than frame-specific appearance.

Reproducibility is insufficient for a control paper. The manuscript omits important details such as policy architecture, optimizer and learning-rate settings, demonstration collection, preprocessing, number of evaluation episodes, normalized-score computation, and checkpoint-selection procedure. The provided compression-layer pseudocode is internally inconsistent: Conv2d outputs compress_dim channels, but BatchNorm2d is instantiated with hidden_dim. Equation 3 also contains conflicting task/visual-prompt notation.

The method is computationally costly relative to the baselines: Table 7 reports 480.1M parameters and 48 ms latency, versus 382.9M and 26 ms for SCR and 303.3M and 11 ms for VC-1. This weakens the characterization of the approach as having minimal overhead, while memory and training costs are not reported.

The experiments cover selected simulated tasks only and do not test real-robot transfer, visual perturbations, unseen environments, or adaptation to new tasks. Because separate prompts and policies are trained per task, the results demonstrate per-task fitting rather than broader task-adaptive generalization. Combined with the missing DINOv2 controls and evaluation bias, these limitations currently outweigh the promising empirical idea.

strengths: The paper presents a well-motivated and useful idea: task-specific learnable prompts and frame-specific dense visual prompts adapt a frozen text-to-image diffusion representation to robotic control. The empirical results are consistently favorable across 12 tasks from three distinct simulated-control suites. ORCA achieves aggregate scores of 74.3 on DMC, 95.2 on MetaWorld, and 65.3 on Adroit, compared with the strongest reported competing aggregates of 70.7, 93.1, and 58.0, respectively.

The comparison includes several relevant alternatives: frozen CLIP, VC-1, and diffusion features, as well as simple captions, learned textual prompts, and TADP-style visual conditioning. This supports the claim that naive textual conditioning is insufficient and that the proposed joint conditioning is useful.

The component ablation is informative: on DMC, task prompts and visual prompts individually improve the null-conditioned diffusion baseline from 68.3 to 69.8 and 70.5, while combining them reaches 74.3. Layer and diffusion-timestep ablations, attention visualizations, and latency/parameter reporting further strengthen the analysis.

The manuscript is generally clear, visually polished, and easy to follow. The distinction among task-agnostic features, textual conditioning, and frame-dependent visual conditioning is communicated effectively.
weaknesses: The most important experimental confound is the additional DINOv2 encoder. ORCA uses both Stable Diffusion and DINOv2, whereas the central baselines generally use one pretrained backbone. There is no direct DINOv2-to-policy baseline, capacity-matched dual-encoder baseline, or alternative feature-fusion baseline. Consequently, the experiments do not fully isolate whether the gains arise from conditioning the diffusion model or simply from adding strong DINOv2 features and trainable projection layers. This is a material limitation of the evidence.

Model selection may bias the reported performance: MetaWorld and Adroit use the best success rate among periodically evaluated checkpoints, but the number of evaluation episodes and any independent validation procedure are not specified. Results use only three seeds, no significance tests or confidence intervals are provided, and several task-level improvements overlap substantially in standard deviation or are ties. Thus, claims such as outperforming prior methods by a 'significant margin' are stronger than the statistical evidence supports.

There are notable numerical inconsistencies. Figure 1 reports ORCA averages of 96.3 for MetaWorld and 68.3 for Adroit, whereas Tables 2 and 3 report 95.2 and 65.3. Table 6 labels t=0 as the default but reports a DMC mean of 70.8, including Reacher-easy at 71.9, rather than the main result of 74.3 and 87.6. Tables 1 and 4 also give different standard deviations for apparently identical SCR and ORCA configurations. These discrepancies should be resolved because they impede confidence and reproducibility.

The proposed explanation that textual prompts fail because of the web-to-control domain gap remains suggestive rather than established. The evidence consists mainly of selected attention-map examples, without quantitative grounding measurements, systematic correlation between grounding and control performance, or comparisons across differing domain gaps. Likewise, the interpretation that particular visual tokens capture task-relevant motion is based on a small qualitative example.

Reproducibility details are incomplete, including the precise policy architecture, optimizer, learning rates, batch sizes, image preprocessing, evaluation-episode counts, token-projection architecture, and complete checkpoint-selection procedure. The compression-layer pseudocode also applies BatchNorm2d(hidden_dim) immediately after a convolution producing compress_dim channels, which is dimensionally inconsistent unless those dimensions happen to match.

Evaluation is confined to a small number of demonstrations in simulated, visually fixed environments. There is no real-robot experiment or systematic test of robustness to camera, appearance, background, or task variation. Together with the roughly 48 ms latency versus 26 ms for SCR and 11 ms for VC-1, this limits conclusions about practical deployment, although it does not negate the demonstrated benchmark contribution.

strengths: The paper identifies a relevant problem: adapting frozen visual representations to individual control tasks without fine-tuning a large diffusion backbone. Combining learned task prompts with frame-dependent dense visual prompts is intuitive and appears novel in this setting.

The empirical results are generally favorable and reasonably broad for simulated control: ORCA is evaluated on 12 tasks from DMC, MetaWorld, and Adroit, with additional single- and multi-task LIBERO-Long results. It improves the reported mean from 68.3 to 74.3 on DMC and from 58.0 to 65.3 on Adroit relative to the unconditional Stable Diffusion baseline; the LIBERO multi-task gain is also substantial.

The study includes useful comparisons against null, hand-written, caption-based, CoOp, and TADP conditions, as well as component, layer, timestep, backbone, vision-encoder, fine-tuning, and efficiency analyses. Reporting three-seed standard deviations is also helpful.

The cross-attention visualizations provide interpretable qualitative evidence that learned task and visual tokens attend to different spatial regions and that the visual tokens change across frames. The manuscript is largely clear and visually well organized.
weaknesses: The main performance attribution is materially confounded by the additional DINOv2 encoder. ORCA combines Stable Diffusion with dense features from another strong pretrained model, while the principal SCR, VC-1, and CLIP baselines use one encoder. The DINOv2-only comparison does not resolve whether gains arise from conditioning the diffusion representation or simply from adding/fusing a second representation and extra capacity. A parameter- and architecture-matched SD+DINO feature-fusion baseline without cross-attention conditioning is needed. The encoder ablation in Table C shows that encoder choice changes the Adroit mean substantially, reinforcing this concern.

The evaluation protocol risks optimistic model selection. For MetaWorld and Adroit, the paper explicitly reports the best success rate among online evaluations conducted every ten epochs, but it does not identify a separate validation set or correction for selecting the best checkpoint on evaluation rollouts. The number of evaluation episodes is also not reported. With only three training seeds, this makes the magnitude and uncertainty of the claimed improvements difficult to assess.

Several conclusions exceed the presented evidence. Cross-attention maps are descriptive and do not establish that erroneous text grounding causes lower control performance or that the web-to-simulation domain gap is the cause. Likewise, claims of consistent gains and a new state of the art are overstated: several MetaWorld tasks are saturated or tied, Relocate ties CLIP, significance is not tested, and only simulated environments plus three selected LIBERO tasks are evaluated.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The manuscript omits important policy and optimization details, including the full policy architecture, observation preprocessing and history, optimizer and learning rates, batch sizes, evaluation episode counts, checkpoint selection, and precise prompt-projection/tokenization procedure. Equation 3 ambiguously repeats the visual-prompt symbol where the task prompt is intended, does not clearly define the loss norm or normalization, and the supplied pseudocode applies BatchNorm2d(hidden_dim) after a convolution producing compress_dim channels, which is inconsistent unless those dimensions happen to match.

The comparison to adaptation methods is not fully controlled: ORCA, LoRA, and RoboAdapter modify different parts of different backbones and have different parameterizations. Moreover, ORCA has 480.1M total parameters and 48 ms latency versus SCR's 382.9M and 26 ms, so the discussion of efficiency is valid mainly for per-task trainable/storage parameters, not total model size or inference cost.

Originality is moderate rather than high: the method primarily transfers established prompt-learning and visual-conditioning ideas to a frozen diffusion representation. The robot-control application and dense frame-wise prompts are useful, but the missing matched fusion baseline prevents the experiments from cleanly isolating the value of the central conditioning mechanism. Overall, the promising breadth and results balance these material attribution and evaluation concerns, placing the paper near the acceptance boundary.

strengths: The problem is relevant: adapting frozen pretrained representations to individual control tasks without full backbone fine-tuning is useful. ORCA is a simple combination of learned task tokens and frame-dependent dense visual prompts injected into Stable Diffusion.

The empirical results are reasonably broad for a simulation study. Across the 12 main tasks, ORCA reports higher means than the strongest conditioning baseline on DMC (74.3 vs. 70.7), MetaWorld (95.2 vs. 93.1), and Adroit (65.3 vs. 58.0). Results are averaged over three seeds and generally include standard deviations.

The component ablation is informative: on DMC, task-only and visual-only prompts improve the SCR baseline mean from 68.3 to 69.8 and 70.5, while combining them reaches 74.3. The manuscript also examines layers, timesteps, visual encoders, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, latency, and a small LIBERO evaluation.

The paper is organized clearly and uses helpful attention visualizations to communicate the intended behavior of its prompts. It also acknowledges that its principal design is tied to U-Net-based Stable Diffusion.
weaknesses: The central attribution is confounded by the addition of a strong DINOv2 encoder. ORCA has 480.1M total parameters and 48 ms latency, versus 382.9M/26 ms for SCR, yet there is no controlled baseline that feeds the same dense DINOv2 features directly to the policy or fuses them with SCR outside cross-attention. Table C varies the auxiliary encoder but does not isolate whether diffusion conditioning is preferable to ordinary feature fusion. Indeed, the reported variant without a vision encoder scores 54.7 on Adroit, below SCR's 58.0. Consequently, the evidence does not establish that the proposed conditioning mechanism, rather than extra pretrained features and capacity, causes the main gains.

The claimed explanation for textual prompting failure is not adequately supported. Text captions slightly improve SCR's aggregate results on both DMC (68.9 vs. 68.3) and MetaWorld (92.5 vs. 90.4), while matching or modestly degrading other cases. A few cross-attention visualizations do not demonstrate that domain-gap-induced misgrounding causes performance changes; no grounding metric, controlled intervention, or analysis across tasks is provided.

The evaluation protocol weakens the quantitative conclusions. MetaWorld and Adroit report the best success rate among periodically evaluated checkpoints, but the manuscript does not state the number of evaluation episodes or explain how checkpoints are selected without using test performance. With only three seeds, several claimed improvements overlap substantially in variance, while MetaWorld is close to saturation. The additional LIBERO study covers only three tasks and gives limited multi-task protocol details.

The originality is moderate rather than strong: task prompts closely follow soft-prompt methods such as CoOp, while visual prompts are projected dense features from an existing frozen encoder. The manuscript demonstrates a useful engineering combination but offers limited new technical insight beyond applying these established mechanisms to robotic control.

Reproducibility is inadequate. Important details such as the policy architecture, observation resolution and preprocessing, optimizer and learning rates, demonstration selection, prompt projection dimensions, positional handling, evaluation rollout count, and precise stochastic treatment of the diffusion input are absent. There are also concrete specification errors: Eq. 3 repeats or swaps task/visual prompt notation, and Algorithm 1 applies BatchNorm2d(hidden_dim) after a convolution producing compress_dim channels, which is invalid unless those dimensions happen to match.

The broad claims exceed the demonstrated scope. The main evaluation is entirely simulated, task prompts are trained for known downstream tasks, and there is no evidence of adaptation to unseen tasks, environments, viewpoints, or real robots. The SVD and SD3 experiments evaluate those backbones as feature baselines rather than applying ORCA to them, so they do not establish the generality of the proposed conditioning approach. Overall, the empirical gains are promising, but the missing capacity-matched DINO feature-fusion control and underspecified evaluation/reproduction protocol are material weaknesses that currently favor rejection.

strengths: The paper identifies a meaningful problem: frozen visual representations are task-agnostic, while ordinary text conditioning can be unreliable in robotic-control imagery. The comparison between null, task-name, and generated-caption conditions provides useful empirical motivation.

ORCA is technically plausible and reasonably original as an adaptation of prompt learning to control: task prompts provide task-level adaptation, while dense, frame-dependent visual prompts condition the frozen diffusion backbone without full fine-tuning.

The evaluation is substantial for a vision-based imitation-learning paper, covering 12 tasks across DMC, MetaWorld, and Adroit, with additional single-task and multi-task LIBERO-Long results. Results are averaged over three seeds and generally improve consistently at the benchmark-mean level.

The gains over the strongest diffusion baseline are meaningful: mean performance improves from 68.3 to 74.3 on DMC, 90.4 to 95.2 on MetaWorld, and 58.0 to 65.3 on Adroit. The component ablation also shows the full task-plus-visual design outperforming either prompt type alone on DMC.

Comparisons against full fine-tuning, LoRA, RoboAdapter, stronger frozen encoders, alternative visual encoders, diffusion timesteps, and U-Net layers provide useful supporting evidence. In particular, the fine-tuning results substantiate the motivation for adapting conditions rather than the full backbone.

The paper is clearly organized and uses informative cross-attention visualizations. It also reports important efficiency costs: ORCA has 480.1M total parameters and 48 ms latency, compared with 382.9M and 26 ms for SCR.
weaknesses: The central attribution is not fully isolated. ORCA adds a large DINOv2 encoder and learned projection, but the paper does not compare against a simple policy that concatenates or fuses DINOv2 features with SCR features without injecting them as diffusion prompts. The visual-encoder ablation shows that external features help, but not that cross-attention conditioning is the reason they help.

The claim that ORCA outperforms all baselines across all 12 tasks is overstated at the task level. Several results are ties or nearly indistinguishable within standard deviations: Drawer is 100 for many methods, Hammer ties SCR and Caption at 98.7, Relocate ties CLIP at 44.0, and multiple DMC gains are small relative to variance. The evidence supports the strongest aggregate means, not uniform task-wise superiority.

Evaluation uses the best success rate among periodic online evaluations. Selecting the best checkpoint using evaluation performance can introduce optimistic bias, and the manuscript does not specify a separate validation protocol, number of evaluation episodes, or uncertainty induced by checkpoint selection.

Reproducibility details are insufficient. Optimizer, learning rates, batch size, policy architecture, image preprocessing, evaluation episode count, and seed protocol are not fully specified. The compression-layer pseudocode also applies BatchNorm2d(hidden_dim) after a convolution producing compress_dim channels, which is dimensionally inconsistent unless those values happen to match.

Some repeated results have unexplained discrepancies. For example, the SCR Reacher standard deviation is 9.9 in Table 1 but 1.7 in Table 4, while Cheetah is 6.4 versus 4.4; ORCA Walker-stand is 1.8 versus 2.3. These inconsistencies should be resolved because only three seeds are used.

The attention visualizations are suggestive but do not establish the proposed causal explanation that textual prompts fail because of incorrect grounding. Better attention localization and control performance may be correlated without the former causing the latter.

Practical validation remains limited to simulation, and the main evaluation uses very few demonstrations. There is no real-robot, camera-shift, or cross-environment study establishing robustness. ORCA also roughly doubles SCR latency, so descriptions such as minimal overhead should be qualified.

There are several correctable technical and presentation errors, including inconsistent notation around Eq. 3, where task and visual prompts are mislabeled, and duplicated discussion of Fig. 6. These do not negate the contribution but weaken precision.
